rv.q: Rosy McEwen is brave, upright, her own woman – and movingly embodies absolute trust right up to the end.
This is a slick, strongly visual yet oddly cold Othello. Fashion trumps sentiment and the verse-speaking is patchy.
That uneasiness, though, is perhaps the triumph of the production.
This version is hot on relevance but it’s never ravishing.
His austere staging is bold in its reframing of the play’s themes, but sometimes stilted in execution.
This is a horribly gripping production.
It's an intense collapse, riding Shakespeare's language to find his own meanings, an extraordinary performance at the heart of a revelatory and relevant production.
His directorial focus is forensic, magnifying the psychodrama at the heart of Shakespeare's play and turning Othello's cognitive turmoil inside out with surgical precision.
Clint Dyer delivers a powerful production with performances both dignified and passionate.
This Is a laudably ambitious production, but one that has jettisoned some of the play's key emotional ballast.

Bringing it into the twenty-first century should work but although the costumes and the setting are contemporary, they still use knives, cudgels and carry flaming torches which is anachronistic and a little confusing.

Playing at three hours long, this Othello does drag in places and for all the lights, torches and a rumbling sound design that add plenty of atmosphere to Dyer’s dystopia, there’s a nagging sense that this production is more style than substance.
Despite its shortcomings, this production would probably do great business on Broadway.
When combined with such rich performances of psychological anguish, this production makes a centuries’-old tale feel vivid and captivating, fresh like a sharp cut.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Dyer's historically significant production, praising the exceptional cast—particularly Terera, McEwen, and Hilton—while questioning whether the bold racial reframing fully delivers on its ambitious vision.
